title: The prince raised by hunters
hook: a prince grows up among forest hunters until one sentence tells him who he is
carry: the seer was never really bound
tomorrow: Who was Patanjali, and what is yoga for?

segments.voice: Yesterday: once truly seen, prakriti ends her dance, the way a dancer bows and leaves the stage.

A baby prince is sent away from the palace and grows up in the forest with a tribe of hunters. He hunts with them, eats with them, and thinks of himself as one of them. Why wouldn't he? Years later, a minister of the king finds him and tells him one sentence: you are the king's son. Nothing about the young man changes, not his face, not his hands. And yet he's no longer a hunter. A later Samkhya text, the Samkhya Sutra, sums up the whole story in a few words: like the king's son.
screen: `RAISED BY HUNTERS.` → `YOU ARE THE KING'S SON.` → `NOTHING CHANGES. EVERYTHING DOES.`

segments.voice: That's Samkhya's last surprise, and the Karika says it outright. In paraphrase: no one is really bound, no one is really released, no one really wanders from life to life. It's prakriti, in her many forms, who is bound, wanders and is released. The I-maker, the mind, the feeling of being stuck all sit on prakriti's side. Purusha, the witness, was never in chains, just as the prince was never a hunter. It only seemed so, the way a clear crystal seems red when a red flower sits beside it. So freedom isn't the witness breaking out. It's the mistake clearing up. How? The Karika says by practicing the principles, the count, again and again, until a knowledge arises in three short steps: I am not, nothing is mine, not I. That isn't despair. It means thinking, owning and the sense of me belong to prakriti, and the witness stops claiming them. The goal has a name: kaivalya, aloneness, the seer standing on its own. Many teachers point out that several Hindu schools share this shape, each in its own words: moksha isn't becoming something new. It's recognizing what you always were. Vedanta names that self differently, and this path will get there. Tomorrow, Yoga takes this map and turns it into a practice.
screen: `NO ONE IS REALLY BOUND.` · `THE PRINCE WAS NEVER A HUNTER.` · `I AM NOT, NOTHING IS MINE.` · `KAIVALYA: THE SEER ALONE.`

segments.voice: Let whatever is here come up, a plan, a feeling, a tightness somewhere, and don't argue with it; let it be colored light near the crystal, and notice the crystal itself stays clear. Thoughts can come and go. If you pray, you can pray quietly while the colors pass.
The Samkhya Karika. Its last word on freedom: the witness was never bound. Prakriti is bound and released, and the seer is left alone, kaivalya.
Your line: the seer was never really bound. The prince was always the king's son. Back tomorrow, same hill.

chat.meaning: Karika 62: no one is really bound or released; prakriti in her many forms is. The witness only seemed caught, like a prince who thought he was a hunter.

tie.story: In the Samkhya Sutra's story, a prince raised by forest hunters is told he's the king's son, and stops living as a hunter.

notes: Last day of the Samkhya block (1171–1180) and a week end (days 1174–1180): the teach looks back over the week.

Karika 62, 64 (nāsmi na me nāham, rendered 'I am not, nothing is mine, not I') and 68 (kaivalya) paraphrased. Translations of 64 vary; confirm the rendering and that the gloss (thinking, owning and the I-sense belong to prakriti) is fair.

The crystal and red flower (sphatika and japa flower) is a stock image in Samkhya-Yoga commentaries (and in Vedanta); it is not in the Karika's verses themselves, and the script presents it without attributing it to the Karika. Confirm the source to cite.
Kaivalya glossed as 'aloneness'; this is a translation, not an etymology. Confirm.
